Chapter 8-5: Linear Regression wrap-up

Regression Assumptions and interpretations

Some requirements for regression to “work”

  1. Variables must vary.

  2. Things should be linear (even if we have to force them)

  3. No omitted variable bias.

1. Variables must vary

Variables must vary

  • Regression models asks “what happens to Y when X changes?”. At a minimum, that means both X and Y should change.
  • This seesm obvious, but it can show up in unexpected ways, especially when we’re including multiple predictors in a model.

Variables must vary

For instance, the DV in this model is 2020 turnout, and I’ve included controls for Biden’s share of the two party vote and Trump’s share of the two party vote…

regC(vep20.turnout ~  biden2020 + trump2020, data=states)

So what happened here?

Variables must vary

  • Adding a control variable is akin to asking “what happens to Y when X changes, hold constant for Z?”

  • But if Z and X don’t vary independently of each other, then its not possible to estimate this. Once I control for Trump’s 2020 vote share, Biden’s 2020 vote share no longer varies:

Variables must vary

  • This problem is called “perfect multicollinearity”, and it make a regression model intractable.

  • Near-perfect collinearity (X almost perfectly predicts Z) can also be a problem, but usually this comes up when we include variables that are almost exact copies.

  • In general, this is only a problem with the independent variables are extremely closely correlated, but it leads to very weird looking results:

Variables must vary

  • Avoid including redundant variables in a model

  • In general, remember parsimony: all else equal, a model with just a few variables is probably better than a model with dozens.

2. Things should be linear

Linearity

Linear regression fits straight lines, but many relationships are non-linear

Linearity

In practice, this is less of a problem than it might appear at first glance: we can make things linear by coding variables differently. For example:

  • If the effect of X on Y depends on values of Z, we can use an interaction term

  • If X has a positive effect at low values but a negative effect at high levels, we might include a quadratic term (x + x^2) in the model

  • Both of these could still be expressed as linear models, even though they’re not strictly linear.

Linearity in categorical variables

We’ll often treated ordered variables as if they’re actually numeric, but the effect of X on Y may not actually linear.

Ordinal variables as numbers

If we remove the “Other” category, we can convert partyid to a number and then treat it as an interval-level variable.

survey$numeric_pid <- as.numeric(survey$party_id)
survey$numeric_pid[which(survey$party_id == "Other")] <- NA
survey$numeric_pid[which(survey$party_id == "Not sure")] <- NA

crosstabC(survey$party_id, survey$numeric_pid)

Ordinal variables as numbers

We can use the numeric variable in a regression model without too much of a problem:

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ numeric_pid , data =survey)

Ordinal variables as numbers

  • A one unit increase in “party ID” is associated with a 1.187 unit increase in supporting Trump’s efforts to end DEI.

  • We know that the effect of moving from being a Democrat to being an independent isn’t strictly linear, but this does capture a rough average.

  • If a variable has 5 or more categories, this is probably fine! and it simplifies your interpretation.

Ordinal variables

What if we’re really skeptical that the effect is numeric?

We have two* options.

  • Option 1: make a dummy and compare 1 group vs. all the rest

  • Option 2: include all categories as dummy variables

  • Option 3: we can use polynomials (X, X^2, X^3…) similar to the way we use an interaction term. But this is usually more trouble than its worth.

Ordinal variables: Option 1

  • Creating a single dummy variable that equals 1 for one or more categories will give us an estimate of the effect of being in that category vs. being in any other category.

  • For instance: this gives us a comparison of anyone who described themselves as a Democrat vs. all other groups (Independents are lumped in with Republicans!)

survey$Democrat<-transformC(type = 'dummy', 
           x= party_id, 
           response = c("Strong Democrat", 
                        "Not very strong Democrat",
                        "Independent Democrat"),
           data = survey,
           confirm = FALSE
           )

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ Democrat, data = survey)

Ordinal variables: Option 2

  • Alternatively, we can just include party_id as is, which will result in the variable being treated as categorical.

  • This means we would interpret every coefficient as the effect of being in that category relative to being in the excluded category (here: Strong Dems)

  • This complicates interpretation, but it doesn’t require as many assumptions about the relationship between X and Y.

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ party_id, data = survey)

Nominal variables

  • If our variables are nominal, then we obviously can’t treat them as numeric! But we can either make a single dummy variable and compare one group vs. the rest:
survey$white<-transformC(type = 'dummy', 
           x=race_eth_combined, 
           response = 'White, non-Hispanic',
           data = survey,
           confirm = FALSE
           )

regC(trump_actions_1 ~ white, data = survey)
  • or create multiple dummies.
regC(trump_actions_1 ~ race_eth_combined, data=survey)

TLDR

For simplicity’s sake:

  • it will usually make sense to just re-code ordinal variables as numbers

  • if you have a nominal predictor, it might make sense to make a single dummy and compare one group vs. all other groups.

3. No omitted variable bias.

Omitted variables

  • To correctly estimate the effect of X on Y, we need to account for all potential confounding variables.

  • Its actually okay if we don’t include everything that explains Y! We should be worried about cases where an omitted variable is correlated with X and Y.

Omitted variables

Using simulated data: the actual equation here is: \(Y = 3X + -3Z + \text{error}\)

What will happen if I use a regression model without controlling for Z? Will I get the correct estimate of the effect of X on Y?

Omitted variables

\(Y = 3X + -3Z + \text{error}\)

Yes (within a small rounding error!)

Omitted variables

  • As long as the omitted variable in independent of X, we can estimate the effect of X without bias. “Z” just causes random noise around the regression line.

  • Our estimate of X becomes biased only when Z is correlated with X and we fail to account for it.

Omitted variables

When Z is correlated with X, we’re no longer able to estimate the effect of X correctly unless we control for Z

Omitted variables

  • % Catholic appears to matter for the percentage of people who smoke in a state

  • But this is probably spurious: cigarette taxes are correlated with both % Catholic and with % smokers, so controlling for this confounding makes the original relationship insignificant.

Omitted variables

  • A key difficulty here: we can’t control for everything! This is why its hard to show causal relationships with observational research.
